idiom_name: for-try loop with try await Task.sleep(for:) and a transient-error classifier
implementation_notes: With structured concurrency the pattern is written out: a loop over the attempt budget calls the async operation, classifies the thrown error and waits with try await Task.sleep(nanoseconds:) or Task.sleep(for: .seconds(n)), which suspends the task without blocking a thread and throws CancellationError if the surrounding task is cancelled - so the loop must let that error propagate rather than catch it. The standard library supplies the delay and the cancellation semantics, not the policy: attempt counts, backoff and the retryable-error decision stay with the caller, and the usual shape is a generic withRetry helper over an async closure. Combine's retry operator (the second variant) covers publisher-shaped work but has no delay or classification, so the async loop is the general answer on modern Swift.
pitfalls: Task.sleep throws CancellationError when the task is cancelled; swallowing it turns cancellation into an endless retry loop and breaks structured concurrency.
Task.sleep guarantees only that the task resumes at or after the instant (system sleep can stretch it), so a total-time budget must be measured with ContinuousClock rather than by summing delays.
Retrying an actor-isolated operation re-enters the actor on every attempt, so state mutated before the failure is replayed - the retried body must be idempotent and reentrancy-safe.
Errors are untyped by default: classification needs a typed error enum or protocol, because a generic catch cannot tell a 503 from a decoding bug.

variants.name: Combine Publisher.retry(_:) operator in a pipeline
variants.idiom_name: publisher.retry(n) with delay/catch operators for pacing and fallback
variants.implementation_notes: For Combine pipelines the operator is the mechanism: publisher.retry(3) recreates the subscription to the upstream publisher when it fails and passes the failure downstream after the last attempt, so the policy is expressed in the pipeline rather than in a loop. Because the operator takes only a count, delay and classification come from the surrounding operators - delay(for:scheduler:) or a custom retryWhen-style operator for pacing, catch for the terminal fallback - and the failure path stays visible in the chain, which is the reason to use it for URLSession data tasks and other publisher-based I/O. For plain async/await code the explicit loop remains the alternative, since the operator cannot express a deadline or a retryable-error predicate by itself.
variants.code_sketch:
cancellable = URLSession.shared.dataTaskPublisher(for: url)
    .retry(3)                                  // recreate the subscription up to 3 times
    .map(\.data)
    .catch { _ in Just(Data()) }               // terminal fallback after the last attempt
    .sink(receiveCompletion: { print($0) }, receiveValue: { print($0.count) })
pitfalls: retry(_:) has no delay and no classification: a pipeline that fails permanently (a 404) repeats the same request immediately, so pacing and a predicate must be added around it.
The operator recreates the upstream subscription, so upstream side effects and per-subscription setup happen again on every attempt.
Retrying on the main scheduler floods it; use a background scheduler and add a timeout operator for the per-attempt budget.
Cancelling the AnyCancellable stops retries, but a sink that ignores completion makes exhaustion invisible - handle receiveCompletion.
